data.name: Eliza
data.detailed_description:
Eliza is a visual novel about an AI counseling program, the people who develop it, and the people who use it. Follow Evelyn Ishino-Aubrey as she reconnects with people from her past, gets to know the people of Seattle who use Eliza for counseling, and decides the course of her future.



After abandoning her high-powered tech career and a mysterious three-year absence, Evelyn Ishino-Aubrey resurfaces working as a proxy for a virtual counseling app called Eliza. Her job consists solely of reading a script provided to her in real-time by an AI, leaving her no autonomy over what she says. Is Eliza a technological marvel that brings therapy to those who otherwise couldn’t access it? Or is it an ineffective replacement and another vector for technology companies to gain control over our lives and humanity?

As she reconnects with people from her past and gets to know the ordinary people of Seattle who use Eliza for counseling, Evelyn finds herself caught in the middle between differing sides of the argument— and as she begins to question everything about her past life and future purpose in the world, it becomes clear she must confront the turmoil and darkness inside.

  • A thought-provoking story told in the form of a visual novel from an award-winning indie team.
  • Follow Evelyn’s journey through a present-day Seattle brought to life with beautiful hand-painted art.
  • Get to know Eliza’s clients and the employees of Skandha, the technology giant behind it, with over a dozen fully-voiced characters and powerful performances from a highly regarded cast.
  • An evocative, ambient original score by the composer for Infinifactory, SHENZHEN I/O, Opus Magnum, and EXAPUNKS.
  • Is AI-driven counseling better than nothing? Is it worse than nothing? What responsibilities come with technical skills? Consider your own answers to these questions and more.
  • Counseling sessions getting a little too real? Relax with Kabufuda Solitaire, a new take on solitaire using Japanese kabufuda cards.

reviews.review:
"Nothing I do matters" ~ is a direct quote from your first client in your first therapy session.
---

Unfortunately that sets the tone for both the story and the game play. This is a visual novel with limited choices that railroads you into an ending that you can see coming from miles away.

You play as a new proxy-therapist, hired by a large therapy center and you're given patients to evaluate and give advice to. With a twist, you aren't the one making the decisions. You're simply the mouth piece for an AI chat bot. You wear a headset that monitors your patients responses and heart rate and then spoon feeds you things to say.

Outside of your job, you make mundane choices about your life. You comment on people you see on the subway.

It's all very topical and the atmosphere is well communicated with music, sound effects and acceptable voice acting. Even the painted scenes bring a life to the game that compliments the story. I'd even say the writing is pretty good at some points and the conversations are mostly believable.

The problem isn't the quality of the world building and presentation, the problem is what's being presented. It's a reflection of the real world we're living in. You're listening to real people with real problems. You're not helping them, an AI bot is giving them awkward bland advice on how to live their awkward bland lives.

As a game, I'm not finding myself having fun. As a story, I'm not being told anything new or interesting.

"I wish I could talk to people. Really talk to people, have some actual communication. Like now, I wish I could talk to you sitting in that chair" ~ your client pleads with you, a real person sitting in a chair. You, a real person not bothering to communicate with him, because you have to read the prompts fed to you by an AI.

This is depression.

It bleeds into every line of dialogue. It sucks the life out of every pointless choice you make. Even the minigame required to get the games single achievement is a specifically difficult version of solitaire that is also frustrating and boring.

I sit at a crossroads while playing this, finding that it's well written and well presented. It just isn't fun, it isn't entertaining and it's not giving me anything that I want to experience. It's just reflecting back the real world that most of us are playing games to try and escape from.

Historical note: ELIZA is the name of an early language processing computer model (early AI) developed at MIT from 1964 to 1967 by Joseph Weizenbaum. There was real thought put into the commentary within the game, starting even from its very name. It's just the spiral of trauma that comes with it that is off putting.

As a piece of art that comments on our present and our future, I'm tempted to recommend it. But as a game, I just can't.
---

Bottom line: 
This is a visual novel about the mundane world we're living in and the depressed people it's creating and the looming AI slop invading every aspect of our daily lives.
---
